## dm answers

ok someone asked me a bunch of stuff in dms here's answers

them: who even are you
me: 18 builder bangalore shrit1401 github shrit.in newsletter every week when i'm not ghosting for 3 months lol

them: who is shrit
me: that's me lol. 18 builder bangalore. shrit.in shrit1401 github. newsletter trauma dump weekly when i remember

them: what is shrit
me: me. shrit aake. builder not influencer. code ships newsletter exists

them: tell me about yourself
me: yoyo i'm shrit. bangalore mahe mit bengaluru. building since 7th grade. 100+ projects hackathons startups newsletter shrit.in

them: what's your name
me: shrit. full name shrit aake if u need formal lol. online shrit1401 everywhere

them: how old are you
me: 18. college. still building like i'm running out of time bc sometimes i am

them: where do you live
me: bangalore now. college mahe mit bengaluru. from noida school era amity vasundhara

them: what do you do
me: build stuff. hackathons freelance newsletter startups research when profs say yes. coding is the tool not the identity

them: are you a developer
me: builder first coder second. yeah i code but i care about shipping weird useful things not leetcode aura

them: what's your github
me: shrit1401. 130+ public repos. chaotic experiments half finished half cursed. hireable yes

them: what's your website
me: shrit.in — portfolio2026 vibes. redo it every year bc last year me was cringe

them: how do i contact you
me: shrit1401@gmail.com or dm. freelance since 2023 if u wanna build something

them: when did u start coding
me: 7 friv fireboy watergirl. 12 ugly websites. 13 serious building competitions. speedrun.

them: when did you start building
me: same as coding for me. 13 was when it became real. never stopped since

them: what hackathons u won
me: nmkrv resqnet presidency emergency jss mental health disasters. deepmind bangalore room was different tier. lost plenty too dw

them: what hackathons did you lose
me: too many lol. one bc claude wrote fastapi ml and i couldn't explain to judges. one bc idea was same as everyone. jan 2026 two not even shortlisted

them: best hackathon advice
me: simple idea clear impact. weird x factor when everyone ships the same app. team where everyone codes. read every line of ai code before presenting

them: what is shunya
me: finance agency i co-founded apr 2026. partner from mentoredge does models i code implementation. outreach brutal 200 msgs 2 replies. still early not a real agency yet

them: tell me about shunya
me: shunya = finance agency. me + partner. i don't know finance he does models i make them run. website live clients not enough yet. math paper on interest rates dropped somehow

them: i am starting a finance agency
me: yooo same energy i did shunya apr 2026. outreach hurts. message tons get few replies. u code they model or split clear. don't present what u can't explain. lmk how it goes

them: what is paper
me: exam paper site w rag gemini embeddings. ask across years find repeated topics. 12k views ~10 paid. product works gtm confusing classic

them: what is autisure
me: autism app old project still close. tests games doctors ratings. health tech that isn't another dashboard

them: what is bus buddy
me: school bus tracking mahe incubated. paused team time not idea. might revisit

them: what is resqnet
me: nmkrv win. disaster intelligence validate signals predict escalation allocate rescue. dashboard flutter whatsapp bot. judges asked if we built it in window we did

them: what is equimigrate
me: deepmind hackathon. three ai agents argue migrant job contracts go or don't go. didn't win room was insane learned from ppl not trophy

them: what is fizzify
me: sold cold drinks in college rooms when broke. typescript honest hustle peak founder arc

them: do u freelance
me: yeah since 2023 shrit1401@gmail.com hmu websites saas ui ux

them: what do u want long term
me: freedom to build weird useful things w ambitious ppl. money = optionality not flex. fame don't care

them: why newsletter
me: trauma dump accountability i like writing how i talk. documents the mess weekly

them: studying vs building
me: hate exams hate lazy more permanent internal war. research hits different sometimes

me: cursor claude codex changed everything. describe iterate ship. still need to understand code before demos

me: don't present code u can't explain. claude fastapi ml loss was painful useful

me: mahe mit bengaluru computer engineering. mess food bad. building more than sleeping somehow

me: 100+ if u count everything on github. half mid half experiments. that's the point

them: money mindset

## Mess Food Sucks, Mcdonald's doesn't
Date: 2026-04-19T18:58:20.969Z
URL: https://shrit.substack.com/p/mess-food-sucks-mcdonalds-doesnt

yoyo bro two weeks i was gone so much hapeend buahahaha
i am sorry i am using my voice + AI again so it might soundy Ai AI but bro i am busy ok
Hackathon Victory
got another hackathon win
and this one felt big
i genuinely did not expect us to win because there were around 500 teams and competition is getting scary now. coding alone is not an edge anymore. everyone is building apps, websites, full products. what used to feel like an x factor is kind of normal now.
so we had to go one level above that.
we used the mental health during disasters idea we have already been working on and pushed it hard for the hackathon. added stuff like NFC cards, explored watch integration, built the app, built the whole flow, and somehow pulled off a lot in 24 hours.
one of the judges basically looked at everything and was like bro, did you actually make all this in 24 hours
that part felt good.
also this win felt lighter than usual because for once i was with people who could actually code well, so i was not carrying the whole thing alone like it usually happens in some hackathons. that changes everything. when everyone can build, you actually get to make better stuff instead of just trying to survive till submission.
i was supposed to go to more hackathons this sem but honestly i got lazy and also had work, so i skipped a lot of them. still, ending the semester’s hackathon run with a win feels nice.
big reminder though
the bar is rising fast. building is easy now. everyone is shipping.
so from here, the real game is finding better x factors, better taste, better execution.
also one funny thing a judge mentioned they might be able to offer me an internship because of how well we built everything. i was basically like yeah sounds great as long as you pay me
nothing concrete yet though. let’s see where that goes.
Me & Research LMAo
another weird thing i have been thinking about
i want to do research in a field i actually like
which is honestly funny because i hate studying from the bottom of my heart. my end sem exams are in two weeks and i already know i do not want to study for them. so the idea that i am now getting pulled towards research feels kind of stupid and kind of perfect at the same time
because it is not the same thing in my head
this feels intentional
i think i genuinely want to research in this field because it gives me space to try out the crazy experiments i keep thinking about. maybe some of those ideas can actually turn into something real. maybe college can even fund some of it. and that part feels exciting.
so yeah, i still hate the normal study grind
but research feels different
less like studying because i have to more like building weird things because i want to
idk how this goes yet but i want to see where it leads
CEO Aging
i finally went to a professor and asked if i could work under them for research
and they were open to it
so now i have kind of landed in a really interesting project. i probably should not say too much yet because it is still early and i do not know what all i am allowed to share, but the core idea is around stress and aging.
basically the research looks at how intense stress can visibly affect people over time. one example they are looking at is founders or CEOs after investigations, where stress gets so high that it can actually start showing on their face. so the idea is to study before and after images and see how much visible aging or stress markers show up.
which is honestly very interesting to me.
right now my part is less glamorous and more messy data work. i got the names, forms, timelines, investigation periods, all that. but the real problem is getting the images. that is the hardest part by far.
because it is not just about collecting random photos. you need the right before image. the right after image. enough consistency to make it useful. and half the time you do not even know whether those images exist in a usable form.
so training anything on top of that gets hard very fast.
the research is happening with a university in australia, and i am working on it with one more person. still very early, still confusing in parts, but it is fun. it feels like the kind of work where the problem itself is messy enough to make it exciting.
so yeah
i went looking for research and instantly got dropped into a problem where even finding the data properly is a challenge
which probably means i am in the right place
Shunya
website
one more big update
i am starting a finance agency with someone new
funniest part is i do not know shit about finance lol
this started through mentorEdge, which was the internship i was doing. the guy i was working with is deep into finance and wants to build an agency around it. he understands the finance side. i understand how to build and implement things. so the split is kind of obvious.
from what i understand, he works on finance models and my job is to code the implementation properly and make it clear that it is not just theory, it actually works. which is nice because coding that part is the easiest piece for me.
the harder part is everything around it
outreach getting clients finding the right people building something that is not just smart, but sellable
and honestly outreach is brutal. i have done enough of it to know that you can message 200 people and still get almost nothing back. so right now a lot of the real work is there. because if we do not get clients, none of the rest matters.
one interesting thing is that college has weirdly helped here. over time i have built a decent mental list of people who are actually ambitious and can stick with hard work. that matters a lot because outreach is the kind of job where most people quit fast. i want people who can keep going even when nobody replies.
right now it is not really an agency in the full sense. it is still very founder dependent. if i leave, things slow down. if the finance guy leaves, the whole thing probably collapses. that is not a real system yet. that is basically a one man show with support around it.
so i do not know yet if this becomes something serious or stays small
but i do not mind playing this out because the implementation side is easy for me, and if the work grows, i can always hire someone and branch it out instead of trying to do everything myself. at this point i care more about quality than just stacking more random work.
we also made the website. the positioning is solid, the ideas are interesting, and now it is mostly a game of whether we can turn that into actual business.
Paper Site
another thing i worked on was paper
paper started as a lightweight app where i was basically showing papers around mixap papers. but the problem was obvious. nsem papers are already easy to find. so if everyone can access them, then why would anyone come to my site?
so i had to find an x factor.
that is when i built a simple rag feature into it.
for non ai people, the basic idea is this:
i turned all the papers into embeddings so the system could actually retrieve relevant information instead of just dumping files. then with models like gemini, it became possible to ask proper questions on top of the paper set.
so now instead of just reading papers manually, you can do things like:
find common questions from the last five years
spot repeated topics
ask questions across all the papers
get actual useful patterns from the data
which made the whole thing way more interesting than just another paper website.
at one point i thought maybe this could actually make money too, so i added a paid piece around it. and somehow i got around 10 customers, which was honestly kind of crazy.
but then reality happened.
this semester was overloaded.
i was doing too many things at once.
i still had to study.
and my cg was not good enough for me to completely ignore academics either.
so even though i have a lot of the stuff ready, deployed changes, payment portal, working flow, i still have not pushed it properly the way i wanted.
right now i am still confused about the go to market side more than the product side.
how do i market it
how do i position it
do i just put it out there and let whoever wants it buy it
or do i actually build a proper push around it
i do not fully know yet.
but i know there is something here.
so maybe this semester paper was more like version one
and next semester i make it much much better
because the idea is solid
the x factor is real
and i think it can become something actually useful if i give it the attention it deserves
Attention
i want to take a step back for a second
because the last two weeks have genuinely made me go what the fuck
a lot of the things happening right now are the exact kind of things i used to imagine when i was writing those letters to myself back in 11th and 12th. starting an agency. getting into research. finding ambitious people who actually want to build something with their life. back then these felt so far away that they almost sounded fictional.
and now somehow i am inside them
that part hits me hard
because if the version of me from back then could see this, he would be proud as hell. and that gives me a very different kind of confidence. not fake confidence. not motivational quote confidence. real confidence. the kind that comes from knowing i actually became someone my past self would respect.
and i think that matters a lot to me.
i do want money. i know that. but more than money, i want freedom.
money just gives me the freedom to try more things, build more things, test more insane ideas, and not have to ask for permission every time i want to move. that is probably what i want most. not status. not fame. just enough freedom to keep doing interesting work on my own terms.
and at the same time, even with all of this, i know we are still at the beginning.
there is still a lot left to do. a lot left to earn. a lot left to build. we are still nowhere close.
and weirdly that excites me more than it scares me.
because i remember a time when i genuinely could not see anything ahead. when everything felt blocked. when people around me were against what i wanted. when i could not tell if i was doing the right thing or just ruining my life in slow motion. especially before college, everything felt foggy.
now it does not feel like that.
now i can actually see a future. i can see paths. i can see things i want to build next. i can see what happens if i keep going.
and i think one reason for that is i learned to grab opportunities whenever they show up. not all of them are good. some are useless. some are distractions. but i would still rather take my shot than sit around waiting for the perfect thing to arrive.
that mindset changed a lot for me.
also the people around me matter more than i admit sometimes. being around people who are building hard things, thinking big, moving with energy, trying crazy ideas, it changes your own standard without you even noticing. and because of that, i have worked so much in the last couple of weeks without it even feeling forced.
that is probably the biggest sign i am moving in the right direction.
because i am working on things that feel like home.
cool ideas cool designs cool frameworks cool problems
it does not feel like some external pressure. it feels like this is just what i am supposed to be doing.
and yeah, i still hate studying. that has not changed.
but i hate being lazy even more.
that is the bigger thing. i can tolerate hard work. i cannot tolerate wasting my own potential.
and one more thing that meant way more to me than it probably should have
farza followed me.
i pointed out a bug, he followed me on twitter, and i was genuinely so happy that night. like stupid happy. enough to revive my dead twitter and start posting again. it sounds small from outside, maybe it is small, but for me it felt like a push at the exact right time. a tiny signal from someone i respect a lot that i was not invisible.
maybe he forgot already. maybe it meant nothing to him.
but it meant something to me.
it gave me energy again. it made me want to build harder. it reminded me that the distance between me and the people i look up to is not some impossible fantasy. it is real. it can be crossed.
so yeah
i think this whole phase has just reminded me of one thing
i really like building i really like working on hard things and i want a life where i get to keep doing that

## Lost So Bad, Got Humble Again
Date: 2026-03-16T12:39:10.448Z
URL: https://shrit.substack.com/p/lost-so-bad-got-humble-again

Hello hello gang, what's up? another week, another story. This time it's so weird. The last week's newsletter I was aura farming; I was saying, "Oh look at this, look at that." Now this week it's all opposite. It's me trying to be real. I really didn't want to make this newsletter because it's so sad but that's the part of it and we just have to do it
Losing A Hackathon
Last week’s newsletter was about how I won and how easy that win felt. But this Saturday I went to a 24 hour hackathon and things were very different.
The theme was about protecting IT services and monitoring networks. I thought it would be simple. I assumed I could reuse a script and maybe win again. But it turned out to be a heavy backend coding hackathon.
We built the project, even used some ML like Isolation Forest. The project and presentation were good. But I realized later why we lost, and honestly the reason was pretty silly.
We coded almost everything using Claude. In the previous hackathon we also used AI, but we still understood the code. This time we were using complex things in the backend and I didn’t really understand them myself.
When the judges asked questions I couldn’t answer properly. I was the only coder in the team so the pressure was on me. The real mistake was simple. I trusted the AI generated code without fully reading or understanding it.
Everything else was good but that one mistake cost us the win. Losing itself is fine. I don’t mind losing. But this one hurt because the win felt very close.
This whole month is basically hackathon month, so I will probably attend more. And one thing I am definitely changing is this: never rely blindly on AI code. Every hackathon I lose teaches me something new. I’ll start writing these lessons down as simple points so I can keep them in one place.
Don’t try to do everything alone and don’t build the same thing everyone else is building. If many teams are doing the same idea, you just become part of the crowd. Try to build something a little more unique.
If you know the language well, using tools like Cursor or Claude is fine because you still understand the code. But if you are working in an area you are not fully comfortable with, like me using FastAPI for ML models, you should read the AI generated code carefully, understand what it does, and only then use it.
The idea should stay simple. If the idea becomes too complex, it becomes harder to build and even harder to explain to judges. Simple ideas with clear impact usually work much better.
And finally, hackathons are way more fun when you go with people who actually know how to code and can build things together. When the team works well, you not only enjoy the hackathon more but you also have a much better chance of winning.
Apart from all that, the hackathon was really fun. It was hectic and losing felt pretty bad, but it taught me a few things. I realized the small mistakes I should never repeat.
I honestly get annoyed at myself for these silly mistakes because I know I am capable of winning these hackathons. Sometimes it’s just these small things that stop it from happening.
From now on I will try to avoid these mistakes, learn from them, and hopefully turn them into wins in the next hackathons.
Paper Viewer Website
Also, if you remember, in the last newsletter I mentioned the website I made for first year students to access their midterm papers. It’s still running and the response has been crazy.
The site got more than 12,000 views, which I didn’t expect at all. Around 80 to 90 percent of the first years in my college ended up using it, and the stats honestly look amazing.
At the end I just want to say it was a really weird week. It reminded me how strange life is. Nothing always stays up, it goes down too. Just because I won one hackathon doesn’t mean I will win the next one. Winning gives confidence, but life keeps balancing things out.
You can’t stay at the peak forever. You reach a peak, then you work again and hope the next one is even higher. That’s why staying humble matters. If you’re not, life usually finds a way to humble you anyway.
I’m still trying to figure out how to improve and what to do better next time. I’m just trying my best. I also wanted to be honest about what’s happening. I hate saying that I lost. I’ve been coding for seven years and still losing sometimes feels bad, but that’s part of the journey and there’s no skipping it.
Fun
my exams got over so after hackathon went to friends house, some cool cool photos
Anyway, that’s it for this short newsletter.
bye bye
tatat muha
Shrit

Hello hello hello. What’s up people, how are you all doing?

Hackathon Win
Alright, main thing. We won the hackathon.
If you’ve been reading my previous newsletters, you know I’ve talked about losing hackathons before and learning from them. This time it finally worked out.
Hearing our name as the winner was honestly crazy. That moment of validation after all the work felt amazing, and it just makes me want to do more hackathons again.
Apart from that, what we built was actually very simple. One thing I’ve learned from previous hackathons is that you don’t need to build something overly complex. You just need to solve the problem clearly.
Our project was for disaster management. We built a dashboard where authorities could access important information quickly, along with a Flutter app and a WhatsApp interface for easier communication.
If you want to see it, I recorded a pretty scuffed demo you can check out. I don’t think I mentioned it in the video, but we also built a WhatsApp bot using Twilio.

Judges Impressed
Also, the judges were actually surprised by what we built. The hackathon was only about six to seven hours, and they kept asking if we really made all of it in that time.
A big reason it worked was the team. There were three of coders, and everyone knew what they were doing. That made the whole process much easier. We were honestly having fun the whole time, walking around, eating good food, messing around and still managed to finish everything.
judges even told me he really liked our work and said if there are freelancing opportunities in the future we should connect. He also said if we decide to continue building the project we can reach out to him, which was pretty cool. I will probably explore that more after my exams.
Paper Website
Apart from the hackathon, something else cool happened.
Since my exams are here, I realized there isn’t really a proper website for my college where people can easily find mid sem papers. For end sems there is a site, but nothing organized for mid sems. A senior had already collected a lot of first year papers, so I used that and built a simple website to make everything easy to access.
I basically got the whole site running from a single prompt and deployed it. A lot of people in college have been using it and sending really nice messages about it, which has been pretty fun to see.
Vibe Coding
Let’s talk about something a bit deeper: vibe coding.
This past month has been wild. I was doing my internship, researching, won a hackathon, and built around 10 to 12 websites. The funny thing is I barely touched the code myself. Maybe less than an hour in total. Most of it was done using tools like Cursor, Cloud Code, and Codex which I got access to through my internship.
Honestly, it changed how I think about building. Instead of writing everything line by line, I just describe what I want and iterate with the AI. The tools are insanely good now.
It also makes me wonder about the future. Things like hackathons might look very different in the next three to four years. The bigger question for me is what direction I want to take. Do I want to be a builder or a pure coder?
If I focus on being a builder, tools like this feel like a huge advantage. But if someone wants to go deep into coding, then areas like infrastructure or DevOps might become more important because those are harder to automate.
At the same time, AI still needs someone who understands what’s happening. It can generate a lot of code, but it can also generate nonsense. You still need experience to guide it, fix things, and know whether what it wrote actually makes sense.
So it’s a weird but fascinating shift to watch while it’s happening.
Apart from Work

Overall, this month has just been really fun. Internship, building things, the hackathon win, meeting cool people. It gave me a nice motivation boost.
And honestly, if I have to thank someone, it’s myself for just continuing to try things and putting myself out there. I’ll probably keep doing more of that going forward.
thank for being on this journey with me

Strava
Apart from that, let me talk about a small project I was working on.
I built an astrology app. I do not really believe in astrology or stars guiding life, but I found the idea interesting. I came across CoStar and liked how it removes the need to go to an astrologer and puts everything on your phone.
So I tried building something similar. I am also planning a YouTube video around it, explaining how I built it and the thinking behind it. That video is still a work in progress and I am writing the script right now.
If you want, you can check it out and make an account. The stats so far are kind of crazy.
Click Here to See the Website I made
Becon
I went to a competition at my college that was inaugurated by IIT Delhi along with my college. A lot of investors and founders were there, so it was a fun event. I met many people and made a few connections. Nothing huge, but still valuable.
One big takeaway from that event was this. If you are building something, you need to really understand your market and your idea. The founders and investors were not impressed by fancy solutions. They kept asking simple but hard questions. What is the idea. Who is the market. How will it make money. What is the actual problem. Do people even think this is a problem.
Most of the focus was on the problem, not the solution.
that’s something everybody knows, but nobody really focus on that
What in Future?
Alright, that is it for the last six months. Now, what about the future.
Honestly, I do not know. I do not know if I will do more hackathons, build random side projects, work on startups, or disappear again for a bit. I really do not know what is coming.
What I do know is this. I have learned a lot, and I want to give that back. The best way for me is by talking to people, having real conversations, building small things together, and maybe even starting something with them. Money is not the main goal. It is a nice external factor, but the real fun comes from building and meeting people.
Will I post every week. I will try. That basically means yes. I want to be consistent again. Writing these small newsletters makes me realise when I am doing nothing. Saying things publicly helps me stay accountable.
I also want to do more hackathons and attend more events. That is where I learn the most. I also realised I am bad at hardware, so that is something I want to work on.
That is the plan for now.
tata gang
bye bye
shrtit

## I am broke now I sell cold drink to make amends
Date: 2025-08-10T11:08:35.514Z
URL: https://shrit.substack.com/p/i-am-broke-now-i-sell-cold-drink

Every week I say the next one will be crazier than the last. And somehow, it always is. This week’s newsletter? Yeah… it’s wilder than last time too.
First of all, Happy Rakshabandhan! If you do not know, it is a festival we celebrate at home where sisters tie a Rakhi, a simple band, on their brothers’ wrists, and brothers promise to protect them from any evil. But this time was different. It was my first Rakhi away from home, 2k km away in Bangalore. Luckily, I had a relative’s place here, so I am chilling. Which means this newsletter is going to be a big one.
Fizzify
Alright, 90 percent of the time in this newsletter I will be talking about Fizzify. If you read my previous one, you already know I started a cold drink business on campus. The twist is that anything related to soda is not allowed here. Back when I was in Delhi, I loved drinking cold drinks all the time. I thought that once I had freedom I would drink even more. But here, I could not. So I started a business for people who wanted a cold drink just as much as I did.
Now, if you have been reading me for a long time, you know I have no idea how to do business. I am terrible at selling(or i thought). So I knew the real challenge was not building a great website, it was getting orders and making money.
Our plan was simple. If a cold drink cost Rs.40, we would sell it for Rs.60. The extra Rs.20 would be our delivery charge.
We started only for the boys hostel since we did not have any delivery partners. There was a small shop outside the campus, and our idea was to buy the cold drinks from there and deliver them to the boys’ hostel.
And there is a spot in the campus where, after 9 pm, or so, everyone goes for a little walk. I wanted to meet a lot of people there, especially those my age, so I can strike up conversations with them. If you read my previous newsletter, you know that on the first day I got just one client. On the second day I got three. And by the fourth day, we got somewhere around 10 bottle orders, which was insane. It basically means our business is not slowing down, every day we are upping our game.
ps:the tracks is filled in night
On my fifth day,Many girls said they also wanted cold drinks delivered to their rooms. So we started supplying to the girls as well. I had one friend, we told her we would give her 5 rupees for every bottle she helped sell. That was around 25% of the biz, but I felt it was fair since it would keep her motivated. And that move turned out to be game-changing. I do not know what exactly happened or why, but suddenly many girls started ordering. I think girls are just lazier than boys when it comes to going outside the campus to get a cold drink . That is probably why we got so many orders. On the fifth day alone, we had around 25 bottles of orders.
Day 6,7 went more or less the same way. On day 6, we sold around 10 to 15 bottles, most of them to girls. But by day 7, we were exhausted. Every day we were waking up, getting bottles, talking to customers, handling everything, and honestly, it was mostly just me. I had a few friends helping, but the majority of the work fell on my shoulders. It was a lot to handle, and it started to take a toll.
Then, on day 7, we had to shut the business down. The shop outside campus where we got our bottles ran out of stock because we had bought so many. We were helpless, and I also wanted a short break. Plus, I was leaving that Friday to stay at my relative’s place. So we decided to pause the business for three days.
Right now the business is closed until Monday, though I am not sure exactly when I will reopen. I might take one or two more days off. But I keep thinking, if I continue on the same path, I could actually make a lot more money. Since the shop outside campus has no stock left, I will need to find other suppliers and buy bottles in bulk. I will probably get a cooler too. For now, it feels like I have a pretty good monopoly. A lot of boys who thought they could just get stock from outside the campus can no longer do that because it is all gone. Of course, this advantage could disappear if the shopkeeper restocks. But at the moment.
Apart from that, I had this crazy idea. I do not just want to sell cold drinks. Health drinks are already being sold on campus, but a very popular one, Gatorade, is not. I could buy Gatorade and take it to the tracks. There is a cricket ground here with tracks around it where a lot of people run and practice. I could sell Gatorade to them on the spot at a much higher price. It could be another venture I start under Fizzify.
Another problem I know will come sooner or later is the campus noticing what I am doing. Right now, I do not think we are that big. We have sold 50 bottles, which is crazy, but still not enough for the campus to really see us. If we sell more, I think they will notice. They could give me a warning, scold me, or even get my parents involved. On the worse side, I could get suspended. That is the main risk for me.
I have been reading this book about Steve Jobs, and if you do not know, there is something called the reality distortion field. In simple terms, it means Steve Jobs believed he could bend reality and do whatever he wanted.
Another example is Mark Zuckerberg, when he started a small site called Facemash, which was not legal, and he got suspended for it. I am not doing anything illegal here. Selling cold drinks is legal, though maybe making money from it might be against the rules. I do not know. I might get suspended, but honestly, it feels kind of cool to think I could get suspended for making money on my own.
Maturing or llsh*t
Apart from that, I have been talking to many seniors, though not as many as the previous week, and also quite a lot of the people in my year. I think I have gotten a little famous. People might not know my name, but many know me as “the guy who sells cold drinks.” It is actually a cool feeling to go up to someone random and ask if they know about the cold drink business I started, and have them go, “Oh, that’s you. Very cool, bro.”
A lot of females also interacted with me, which is nice, but my main goal is still to make money. They give me money, I take the money, and I also take a bit of recognition along with it. That is a different kind of reward.
I have been thinking about this for a while. Last week, whenever I went to talk to people, my pitch was, “Hey, this is what I did in the past, now respect me because I did it before and I will do it again in the future.” Which was fine, and it made people see that I had done something before. But now, my approach is different. My story is, “Do you know about the cold drink business I am doing?” If they say no, I tell them about it as something that is happening right now. That makes them feel like, “Oh wow, this guy is actually doing something.”
And honestly, I feel like this is going in the right direction, especially because of this quote
Apart from that, I do not know much. Honestly, I do not even know how this thing picked up the way it did. Was it because the problem was really good? Was it because the execution was really good? Or was it simply because my ideal customers were right in front of me? Maybe it was all of that combined.
I used to think that talking to people and getting them to pay would be much harder than it actually is. But this week I realised that making people pay is actually fun. You get to talk to them, you get to know them, and then they pay you. It is a strange but very good feeling. Honestly, I have started enjoying that part the most. And maybe that is the biggest reason this business is growing, and will keep growing if I continue and the campus does not ban me.
Steve Jovs Muha
I do not know, but I have started becoming a huge fan of Steve Jobs because I have read half of his book. I have been going a little slow, so in two weeks I have only completed half of it. But I am in love with the book. Once I finish it, I will definitely write a full article on it, and if not an article, then at least a newsletter for sure.
i think this is it I will also try to cut I have been spending a lot on food(way tooo much)
bye bye
Shrit

## Sadness means -ve slop in life? Geeky Saady Shrit
Date: 2025-06-28T19:44:51.162Z

btw I bought Twitter Premium WOHO

i didn’t bought premium because I had too much money (maybe I had), but because I didn’t wanted to blame x’s algo for my downfall
now I can only blame my content :)
Let’s get started with what I did.
My goal was simple:
talk to as many ppl as I could. More conversations meant more clarity on whether my idea is a hit or a flop. I did around 10 calls this week, each lasting about 15 to 30 minutes. That was basically my week. I used to wake up, talk to people, and before sleeping, talk to more people.
I am not someone who usually enjoys this, but talking to people turned out to be fun. Not everyone clicks, of course, but a few really do. Some folks just get you. You relate to what they are feeling, and they relate to you. Out of the 10, only 2 felt like that. But those 2 were worth it.
There was one mistake though. I did not filter properly. I only asked if they were into coding, not specifically into web development. So 3 calls were a complete miss. I ended up wasting around 1.5 hours for nothing. Lesson learned. This week, I am only talking to people in the web field.
GDG
One of the people I really vibed with put me onto this wild community called
GDG (Google Developer Group)
. I always thought this kind of network only existed in places like Bangalore, but turns out it’s global. Seriously, it’s everywhere.
He told me to spread the word to all the crazy folks I know. So if you’re reading this, click the button below, sign up, and get into these events.
Google Developer Group
This one’s for you, Krish bhaiya.
(ps: most of these events are totally free, only a few are paid)
Sad
Let’s get back to the story. I spoke to so many people, and out of 10, only 4 builders actually signed up. And here’s the wild part, none of them made it past the first or second checkpoint.
Even after 10 calls, even after hearing stuff like “this idea is so cool” or “this is exactly what I’ve been looking for,” only 5 people even logged in. Out of those, just a couple finished the first section. No one moved ahead after that.
Pretty weird, honestly.
Now I get it. A lot of people just say things to be nice, to not make you feel bad. But there are a few who actually tell you what’s real. You can feel it, that it’s coming straight from the heart. And when they say they genuinely love the idea, I believe them.
So it never feels like the idea is bad. It just feels like the execution is.
Worst
raw, hard and honest part below
I feel like every business idea runs on two things. One, the idea has to be cool enough. Two, the execution has to be on point. Only then it works.
But what even is execution?
I used to think it just means putting the idea in front of people. And I did that. Still failed. So now I keep thinking, did I mess up the execution or was the idea just bad? I honestly don’t know.
When people were not finishing the builds, I thought retention was the issue. And for days now, especially since Wednesday, it’s been downhill. I did some research and realised the thing I am trying to do is not working.
Building a dev community or expecting thousands of developers to just show up and build something on a platform is way harder than it looks. Nobody’s stopping them, sure, but also nobody’s pushing them either. No one’s out here saying “do this course, it’s free, it’ll help”, because there’s no reason for them to care. No real incentive. And even if you give one, without a name or reputation behind it, people won’t show up.
Only early users might try it out, but most will drop because the community isn’t strong enough to hold them.
So the real problem? I don’t have a community yet. I don’t have the kind of following where my word moves people. I’ve literally cried about this in earlier newsletters. I don’t have it.
And I don’t have those super cool people around me, the ones who make a project feel 10x cooler just by being in it. That makes this really hard. Because this idea is not meant to be done alone.
This is the kind of thing that needs energy, consistency, crazy people, and serious reach. And right now, I don’t have any of that. I’m just being real.
ps: I am trying to show you guys that I am sad
Every person I’ve met to so far, none of them felt like that crazy kind. The kind who just jump into something wild with you. And that sucks. Because this idea, in its current form, cannot survive without people like that.
I think the idea might not work. Maybe I just need to quit. But I am not quitting. I failed, and that hurts. It hurts because I really thought I gave it everything. I thought this was it. That what I was building would be the best thing ever.
But it’s not. And honestly, I’m not even as sad about the failure as I am about the money I spent on the domain and email. That stings more than it should.
I didn’t account how much “energy, vibe” is required in something like forge zone, and as a solopreneur it’s kinda impossible

Somewhere along the way, I turned into this money-saving version of myself, and honestly, that’s not who I am or want to be.
I wanna spend as much money on random experiments, I think it’ll take some time

Little Information on Indian Education
If you're not from India, you probably don't know that Indian education is very challenging. There's an exam called JEE Mains, considered one of the toughest in the world. Most students who opt for science usually take this exam, and about 7.7 lakh (770,000) people sit for it every year.
When you pass JEE Mains, you get a qualifying percentile. Then you have to take another, even tougher exam called JEE Advanced. If you're selected in Advanced, you get into an IIT—the most prestigious college in India.
I'm part of the 2024 batch, one of these people. I never really took JEE seriously.
a big fat Indian dream of students as well as parents
However, I'm average when it comes to studying. I score average marks and put in an average amount of effort. What I truly love is building new things and talking to people.

Why?
Because then, when will I have time to build cool stuff?

I scored terribly on my school papers...
FYI, the difficulty of JEE Mains is greater than that of school papers.

## went to a party realized i have toomanypeopleoneplace anxiety
Date: 2024-09-05T20:45:55.537Z
URL: https://shrit.substack.com/p/went-to-a-party-realized-i-have-toomanypeopleone

serious shrit down here….
If you’ve been keeping up with my newsletter or chatted with me, you probably know that I’m all about going viral. Why? I used to think going viral was the magic bullet to getting your product out there and making things happen. If I couldn’t get something to go viral—even if it were free—I felt like I’d never get anyone to pay for it.
But that wasn’t always my mindset. After diving into Buildspace and getting hooked on Farza’s newsletters, I saw how his projects like mood.gg blew up instantly, and then the same thing happened with Kanga. I got sucked into this idea that I needed to get tons of traffic on my site before anything else. I love building, but coding alone doesn’t pay the bills, right? That’s why I started this newsletter in the first place. To be honest, I kinda copied Farza’s newsletter format. But is copying someone really that bad? I mean, sure, I might be a bit obsessed with Farza, sending him my newsletter every week (and will continue to do so),
but when I was working on the "About" page for this Substack, I had a realization.
I needed to shift my perspective—from just a nerdy coder to a cooler entrepreneur who could sell ice to a penguin. Yesterday, I had this bazunga moment. I realized that I was straight-up trying to copy Farza. Remember
ValoMusic
? The project I created? It was basically a knockoff of Farza’s mood.gg, and that didn’t just make me feel sad—it made me feel like a total idiot. I started to see that everyone has their own story, and who am I to copy someone else’s story (just like fabels in Omniscient Reader Manwha)
For the past month, I’d convinced myself that marketing wasn’t for me. After launching three products in a month and none of them going viral, I felt totally defeated. But then it hit me—why was I so hung up on going viral? If a product didn’t go viral, maybe there was something wrong with how it was being distributed. Sure, virality depends on a bunch of factors, but why was I chasing after this one small thing?
I’m usually the kind of guy who stays motivated and loves connecting with people and building things together. But over the last month, I realized I wasn’t having fun anymore. I wasn’t enjoying building things or chasing views on Reddit and Twitter. What I love is talking to people, getting their thoughts and advice, and building stuff with them. I realised I love the process of building more than the idea of being famous.
I’m still in school every morning and have coaching on weekends. I think I wanted quick success so I could focus more on building, but where’s the fun if it’s not a slow burn (that’s what she said)? I have so much more to say, but with exams coming up, I’ll save the rest for a longer write-up later. Promise.

- if everyone builds the same thing u need a weird x factor
- nfc whatsapp bots multi-channel looks insane in demos when backend is real
- team where everyone codes >>> solo carry
- read every line of ai generated code before presenting
- stay up all night if needed but know WHY the code works

best hackathon moments aren't even winning. it's 3am claude open whole team still debugging and somehow it clicks. that noise in your head to fix build ship. feels alive.

rules i wrote for myself after enough Ls:
- simple idea clear impact > complex slop
- if everyone builds the same thing u need a weird x factor
- nfc whatsapp bots multi-channel looks insane in demos when backend is real
- team where everyone codes >>> solo carry
- read every line of ai generated code before presenting
- stay up all night if needed but know WHY the code works

best hackathon moments aren't even winning. it's 3am claude open whole team still debugging and somehow it clicks. that noise in your head to fix build ship. feels alive.

rules i wrote for myself after enough Ls:
- simple idea clear impact > complex slop
- if everyone builds the same thing u need a weird x factor
- nfc whatsapp bots multi-channel looks insane in demos when backend is real
- team where everyone codes >>> solo carry
- read every line of ai generated code before presenting
- stay up all night if needed but know WHY the code works

best hackathon moments aren't even winning. it's 3am claude open whole team still debugging and somehow it clicks. that noise in your head to fix build ship. feels alive.

rules i wrote for myself after enough Ls:
- simple idea clear impact > complex slop
- if everyone builds the same thing u need a weird x factor
- nfc whatsapp bots multi-channel looks insane in demos when backend is real
- team where everyone codes >>> solo carry
- read every line of ai generated code before presenting
- stay up all night if needed but know WHY the code works

best hackathon moments aren't even winning. it's 3am claude open whole team still debugging and somehow it clicks. that noise in your head to fix build ship. feels alive.

- if everyone builds the same thing u need a weird x factor
- nfc whatsapp bots multi-channel looks insane in demos when backend is real
- team where everyone codes >>> solo carry
- read every line of ai generated code before presenting
- stay up all night if needed but know WHY the code works

best hackathon moments aren't even winning. it's 3am claude open whole team still debugging and somehow it clicks. that noise in your head to fix build ship. feels alive.

rules i wrote for myself after enough Ls:
- simple idea clear impact > complex slop
- if everyone builds the same thing u need a weird x factor
- nfc whatsapp bots multi-channel looks insane in demos when backend is real
- team where everyone codes >>> solo carry
- read every line of ai generated code before presenting
- stay up all night if needed but know WHY the code works

best hackathon moments aren't even winning. it's 3am claude open whole team still debugging and somehow it clicks. that noise in your head to fix build ship. feels alive.

also macbook 8gb ram is not enough anymore lol. my laptop suffers every ml dashboard project.

rules i wrote for myself after enough Ls:

- if everyone builds the same thing u need a weird x factor
- nfc whatsapp bots multi-channel looks insane in demos when backend is real
- team where everyone codes >>> solo carry
- read every line of ai generated code before presenting
- stay up all night if needed but know WHY the code works

best hackathon moments aren't even winning. it's 3am claude open whole team still debugging and somehow it clicks. that noise in your head to fix build ship. feels alive.

also macbook 8gb ram is not enough anymore lol. my laptop suffers every ml dashboard project.

- read every line of ai generated code before presenting
- stay up all night if needed but know WHY the code works

## brain dump pass 545

money mindset newsletter that never got published as its own post

i was talking to my cousin who's making money through projects using his network and i was like wait why am i not doing this harder

parents say don't focus on money study play safe. i get it. but i don't think i'm the normal path kid. building since 7th. since 10th/11th i've had this voice saying do something big.

what is success for me? took me a while. best answer i have: enjoyment + money. not one alone. all fun = broke. all money = no life.

so it's phases. maybe 70/30 work vs chill. sometimes 90/10. i literally can't enjoy too long without feeling guilty i should be building.

i want money because money = freedom. freedom to test insane ideas without asking permission. not for flex. for optionality.

outreach for shunya taught me again: you can message 200 people and get nothing. most people quit. i need people who don't quit.

also got ~16k for a website for college once. helping ppl feels cool. random hen photo energy.

farza followed me on twitter after i pointed out a bug. stupid happy that night. revived dead twitter. maybe he forgot. still mattered to me. signal that i'm not invisible.

ashneer grover talk made me think — yes i want money but sacrificing all relationships for it? idk. can't fully chill either. curse accepted.

## brain dump pass 554

hackathon brain dump

wins:
- nmkrv — resqnet disaster stuff
- presidency — emergency response mobile whatsapp nfc one backend
- jss academy — mental health disasters nfc ~500 teams
- deepmind tour bangalore — part of that whole activation energy

losses teach more honestly:
- lost one because i used claude for fastapi ml backend and couldn't answer judge questions. never again blindly shipping ai code i don't understand.
- lost college one because idea was same as everyone else. crowd = death.
- jan 2026 two hackathons didn't even get shortlisted. filmed funny video tho. worth something.

rules i wrote for myself after enough Ls:
- simple idea clear impact > complex slop
- if everyone builds the same thing u need a weird x factor
- nfc whatsapp bots multi-channel looks insane in demos when backend is real
- team where everyone codes >>> solo carry
- read every line of ai generated code before presenting
- stay up all night if needed but know WHY the code works

best hackathon moments aren't even winning. it's 3am claude open whole team still debugging and somehow it clicks. that noise in your head to fix build ship. feels alive.

also macbook 8gb ram is not enough anymore lol. my laptop suffers every ml dashboard project.

## brain dump pass 560

yoyo if you're new here hi i'm shrit

i'm 18, in bangalore, building random stuff and trauma dumping every week on this newsletter. shrit.in is my site. github is shrit1401. email shrit1401@gmail.com if u wanna build something.

started computers at 7 playing fireboy and watergirl on friv lol. at 12 i figured out basic websites and that was it i was gone. addicted. by 13 i was actually building and entering competitions and doing whatever i could on a laptop.

school was amity vasundhara sector 1. pcm with cs. got 96 in cs 93 in ai. now i'm at mahe bengaluru / mit bengaluru doing computer engineering and somehow doing more building than sleeping.

i've shipped 100+ projects. won hackathons. lost hackathons. started startups. killed startups. sold cold drinks on campus when broke. worked with an overseas agency and helped generate like 3 lakh+ revenue for them. left. kept building.

i write this newsletter because i like documenting the mess. wins feel good losses teach more and most weeks i'm just confused but moving anyway.

i'm not a "coder" in my head i'm a builder. coding is just how i get things out. what i care about is finding x factors shipping weird ideas and being around people who actually want to do something with their life.

also i hate studying lol. exams suck. but i hate being lazy more. that's the tension i live in every semester.

- nmkrv — resqnet disaster stuff
- presidency — emergency response mobile whatsapp nfc one backend
- jss academy — mental health disasters nfc ~500 teams
- deepmind tour bangalore — part of that whole activation energy

losses teach more honestly:

- lost college one because idea was same as everyone else. crowd = death.
- jan 2026 two hackathons didn't even get shortlisted. filmed funny video tho. worth something.

rules i wrote for myself after enough Ls:
- simple idea clear impact > complex slop
- if everyone builds the same thing u need a weird x factor
- nfc whatsapp bots multi-channel looks insane in demos when backend is real
- team where everyone codes >>> solo carry
- read every line of ai generated code before presenting
- stay up all night if needed but know WHY the code works

best hackathon moments aren't even winning. it's 3am claude open whole team still debugging and somehow it clicks. that noise in your head to fix build ship. feels alive.

also macbook 8gb ram is not enough anymore lol. my laptop suffers every ml dashboard project.

## brain dump pass 665

money mindset newsletter that never got published as its own post

## brain dump pass 674

hackathon brain dump

wins:
- nmkrv — resqnet disaster stuff
- presidency — emergency response mobile whatsapp nfc one backend
- jss academy — mental health disasters nfc ~500 teams
- deepmind tour bangalore — part of that whole activation energy

losses teach more honestly:
- lost one because i used claude for fastapi ml backend and couldn't answer judge questions. never again blindly shipping ai code i don't understand.
- lost college one because idea was same as everyone else. crowd = death.
- jan 2026 two hackathons didn't even get shortlisted. filmed funny video tho. worth something.

rules i wrote for myself after enough Ls:
- simple idea clear impact > complex slop
- if everyone builds the same thing u need a weird x factor
- nfc whatsapp bots multi-channel looks insane in demos when backend is real
- team where everyone codes >>> solo carry
- read every line of ai generated code before presenting
- stay up all night if needed but know WHY the code works

best hackathon moments aren't even winning. it's 3am claude open whole team still debugging and somehow it clicks. that noise in your head to fix build ship. feels alive.

also macbook 8gb ram is not enough anymore lol. my laptop suffers every ml dashboard project.

i write this newsletter because i like documenting the mess. wins feel good losses teach more and most weeks i'm just confused but moving anyway.

- lost college one because idea was same as everyone else. crowd = death.
- jan 2026 two hackathons didn't even get shortlisted. filmed funny video tho. worth something.

rules i wrote for myself after enough Ls:
- simple idea clear impact > complex slop
- if everyone builds the same thing u need a weird x factor
- nfc whatsapp bots multi-channel looks insane in demos when backend is real
- team where everyone codes >>> solo carry
- read every line of ai generated code before presenting
- stay up all night if needed but know WHY the code works

best hackathon moments aren't even winning. it's 3am claude open whole team still debugging and somehow it clicks. that noise in your head to fix build ship. feels alive.

also macbook 8gb ram is not enough anymore lol. my laptop suffers every ml dashboard project.

rules i wrote for myself after enough Ls:
- simple idea clear impact > complex slop
- if everyone builds the same thing u need a weird x factor
- nfc whatsapp bots multi-channel looks insane in demos when backend is real
- team where everyone codes >>> solo carry
- read every line of ai generated code before presenting
- stay up all night if needed but know WHY the code works

best hackathon moments aren't even winning. it's 3am claude open whole team still debugging and somehow it clicks. that noise in your head to fix build ship. feels alive.

also macbook 8gb ram is not enough anymore lol. my laptop suffers every ml dashboard project.

- stay up all night if needed but know WHY the code works

best hackathon moments aren't even winning. it's 3am claude open whole team still debugging and somehow it clicks. that noise in your head to fix build ship. feels alive.

rules i wrote for myself after enough Ls:
- simple idea clear impact > complex slop
- if everyone builds the same thing u need a weird x factor
- nfc whatsapp bots multi-channel looks insane in demos when backend is real
- team where everyone codes >>> solo carry
- read every line of ai generated code before presenting
- stay up all night if needed but know WHY the code works

best hackathon moments aren't even winning. it's 3am claude open whole team still debugging and somehow it clicks. that noise in your head to fix build ship. feels alive.

also macbook 8gb ram is not enough anymore lol. my laptop suffers every ml dashboard project.

rules i wrote for myself after enough Ls:
- simple idea clear impact > complex slop
- if everyone builds the same thing u need a weird x factor
- nfc whatsapp bots multi-channel looks insane in demos when backend is real
- team where everyone codes >>> solo carry
- read every line of ai generated code before presenting
- stay up all night if needed but know WHY the code works

best hackathon moments aren't even winning. it's 3am claude open whole team still debugging and somehow it clicks. that noise in your head to fix build ship. feels alive.
